---
title: "Inspect the model"
subtitle: "Read HRF shapes, regressor timing, design structure, and correlations."
jupyter: python3
---


A fit can finish successfully even when its design describes the wrong
experiment. Plot the model before interpreting the statistics: check the HRF
shape, the timing of each regressor, the full design, and correlations between
columns. These helpers return Matplotlib figures or axes, so labels, limits,
and export remain under your control.

On a narrow screen, scroll plots horizontally to read their labels. Select a
plot to open a complete view.

## Compare HRF shapes

`plot_hrfs` overlays HRF objects. Normalization helps compare shapes, but it
removes their native amplitude differences. For a multi-basis HRF, this helper
shows only the first basis column; use `plot_hrf` to inspect every basis.

::: {#e368609b .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='8' execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import fmrimod as fm
from fmrimod.hrf import get_hrf
from fmrimod.plotting import plot_hrf, plot_hrfs
from fmrimod.spec import compile as compile_spec
from fmrimod.spec import hrf
from fmrimod.visualization import (
    correlation_map, design_map, plot_design_matrix, plot_sampling_frame,
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
plot_hrfs(get_hrf("spmg1"), get_hrf("gamma"), normalize=True,
          labels=["SPM canonical", "gamma"], ax=ax)
ax.set_title("")
ax.set_xlabel("Time after event (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Normalized response")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![SPM canonical and gamma HRFs, normalized separately to unit peak. Choose a response model for the experiment, and preserve its amplitude convention when comparing coefficient values.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){fig-alt='Overlaid SPM canonical and gamma HRF curves with equal unit peaks but different response shapes.'}
:::
:::


## Follow events into regressors

Compile the event specification against the acquisition times. This small
example has twelve alternating face and scene events. Its figures describe
a design; no BOLD data have been fitted.

::: {#995cf44c .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
events = pd.DataFrame({
    "onset": np.arange(4.0, 100.0, 8.0),
    "condition": ["face", "scene"] * 6,
    "duration": 2.0,
})
sampling = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=120, TR=1.0)
event_model, _ = compile_spec(
    hrf("condition", basis="spmg1"), data=events, sampling_frame=sampling,
)
```
:::


::: {#48a9f2b6 .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='8' execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plot_design_matrix(event_model, figsize=(8, 3.2))
ax.set_title("")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Alternating face and scene regressors. Check event order, response delay, overlap, and the end of the run against the experiment's timing table.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){fig-alt='Face and scene regressors plotted over 120 seconds. Alternating responses overlap after convolution with the HRF.'}
:::
:::


## View the design as a matrix

A heatmap makes missing columns, constant columns, and blocks of repeated
structure easier to see. Color represents the value of a regressor at a
sample, not an effect estimate.

::: {#cca3e7c6 .cell fig-height='4.4' fig-width='6' execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = design_map(event_model, figsize=(6, 4.4), cmap="viridis")
ax.set_title("")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The same event design as a heatmap. The two views show identical regressors: the line plot emphasizes timing; the matrix emphasizes column structure.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='Design heatmap with acquisition samples as rows and the face and scene regressors as columns, showing alternating bands of response.'}
:::
:::


## Inspect column correlations

A correlation map helps identify regressors that share much of their time
course. It does not establish whether a contrast is estimable, and centering
a modulator does not guarantee orthogonal convolved regressors. The
[design guide](design-matrices.qmd) explains how to inspect column metadata;
the [modulator guide](parametric-modulators.qmd) explains centering.

::: {#68d13a57 .cell fig-height='3.8' fig-width='5' execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = correlation_map(event_model, figsize=(5, 3.8), annot=True)
ax.set_title("")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Pairwise correlations in the example event design. Both columns describe alternating conditions, so their negative correlation follows from the schedule. Baseline and nuisance columns are not included in this event-only matrix.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two-by-two correlation matrix for the face and scene regressors, with unit diagonal entries and negative off-diagonal correlations.'}
:::
:::


## Check the acquisition grid

The timeline view shows run spans. The grid view shows sample indices within runs. Use the timeline when
comparing run durations with differing repetition times.
Neither view resamples the data.

::: {#cf6f92f9 .cell fig-height='2.6' fig-width='8' execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
multi_run = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=[40, 30], TR=[1.0, 1.5])
fig, ax = plot_sampling_frame(multi_run, style="timeline", figsize=(8, 2.6))
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Two example runs with different TRs. Forty samples at 1 s span 40 s; thirty at 1.5 s span 45 s. This timeline shows run spans, not individual acquisition ticks.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){fig-alt='Timeline of two consecutive runs: forty seconds for forty samples at TR 1 second, then forty-five seconds for thirty samples at TR 1.5 seconds.'}
:::
:::


## Inspect fitted estimates

The same approach applies after fitting. Follow these worked examples:

- [Contrast weights](contrasts.qmd#inspect-the-resolved-weights): see exactly
  which columns receive positive, negative, and zero weights.
- [Rank and residuals](linear-model.qmd#inspect-rank-and-conditioning):
  inspect numerical rank and compare observed signals with their fitted values.
- [Recovered effects](linear-model.qmd#plot-the-recovered-effect): compare
  estimates and standard errors with the simulated coefficients.
- [HRF estimation](estimating-hrfs.qmd): compare fitted curves with a known
  generating response and inspect pointwise uncertainty.
- [Single-trial estimates](single-trial.qmd#plot-trial-estimates): inspect
  trial amplitudes and their standard errors.
- [Group examination](group-diagnostics.qmd): distinguish surprising maps
  from influential subjects under a specified group model.
- [FIAC brain maps](real-data-fiac.qmd): reconstruct spatial contrast results
  using retained image geometry.

For a reusable figure, keep the returned object and call
`fig.savefig("design.svg", bbox_inches="tight")`. Supply an existing `ax`
to HRF helpers when composing panels; design helpers create their own figure
and accept `figsize`.
